texts.90.6: She led the horse into the dark stable, took his bridle off, put a halter on him, slackened his girths, and gave him a feed of corn -- all in the dark; which things done, she and her lover set out for the Horn.
texts.90.7: The whole night seemed thinking of the day that was gone. All doing seemed at an end, yea God Himself to be resting and thinking. The peace of it sank into their bosoms, and filled them so, that they walked a long way without speaking. There was no wind, and no light but the starlight. The air was like the clear dark inside some diamonds. The only sound that broke the stillness was the voice of Kirsty, sweet and low -- and it was as if the dim starry vault thought, rather than she uttered, the words she quoted:--
texts.90.12: At a certain spot on the ridge of the Horn, Francis stopped.
texts.90.13: ''This is whaur ye left me this time last year, Kirsty," he said;" -- left me wi' my Maker to mak a man o' me. It was 'maist makin me ower again!"
texts.90.14: There was a low stone just visible among the heather; Kirsty seated herself upon it. Francis threw himself among the heather, and lay looking up in her face.
texts.90.15: "That mother o' yours is 'maist ower muckle for ye, Francie!" said Kirsty.
texts.90.16: "It's no aften, Kirsty, ye tell me what I ken as weel's yersel!" returned Francis.
texts.90.17: "Weel, Francie, ye maun tell me something the night! -- Gien it wudna mismuve ye, I wad fain ken hoo ye wan throu that day we pairtit here."
texts.90.18: Without a moment's hesitation, Francis began the tale, giving her to know, however, that in what took place there was much he did not understand so as to tell it again.
texts.90.19: When he made an end, Kirsty rose and said,
texts.90.20: "Wad ye please to sit upon that stane, Francie!"
texts.90.21: In pure obedience he rose from the heather, and sat upon the stone.
texts.90.22: She went behind him, and clasped his head, round the temples, with her shapely, strong, faithful hands.
texts.90.23: "I ken ye noo for a man, Francis. Ye hae set yersel to du His wull, and no yer ain: ye're a king; and for want o' a better croon, I croon ye wi my twa han's."
texts.90.24: Little thought Kirsty how near she came, in word and deed, to the crowning of Dante by Virgil, as recorded toward the close of the "Purgatorio."
texts.90.25: Then she came round in front of him, he sitting bewildered and taking no part in the solemn ceremony save that of submission, and knelt slowly down before him, laying her head on his knees, and saying,
texts.90.26: "And here's yer kingdom, Francis -- my heid and my hert! Du wi' me what ye wull."
texts.90.27: "Come hame wi' me, and help save my mother," he answered, in a voice choked with emotion.
texts.90.28: "I wull," she said, and would have risen; but he laid his hands on her head, and thus they remained for a time in silence. Then they rose, and went.
texts.90.29: They had gone about half-way to the farm before either spoke. Then Kirsty said, --
texts.90.30: "Francie, there's ae thing I maun beg o' ye, and but ane -- 'at ye winna desire me to tak the heid o' yer table. I canna but think it an ungracious thing 'at a young wuman like me, the son's wife, suld put the man's ain mother, his father's wife, oot o' the place whaur his father set her. I'm layin doon no prenciple; I'm sayin only hoo it affecs me. I want to come hame as her dochter, no as mistress o' the hoose in her stead. Ye see, Francie, that'll gie ye anither haud o' her, agea disgracin o' hersel! Promise me, Francie, and I'll sune tak the maist pairt o' the trouble o' her aff o' yer han's."
texts.90.31: "Ye're aye richt, Kirsty!" answered Francis. "As ye wull."
texts.91.1: The next morning, Kirsty told her parents that she was going to marry Francie.
texts.91.2: "Ye du richt, my bairn." said her father. "He's come in sicht o' 's high callin, and it's no possible for ye langer to refuse him."
texts.91.3: "Eh! what am I to du wantin ye, Kirsty?" moaned her mother.
texts.91.4: "Ye min', mother," answered Kirsty, "hoo I wad be oot the lang day wi Steenie, and ye never thoucht ye hadna me!"
texts.91.5: "Na, never. I aye kenned I had the twa o' ye."
texts.91.6: "Weel, it's no a God's-innocent but a deil's-gowk. I'll hae to luik efter noo, and I maun come hame ilka possible chance to get hertenin frae you and my father, or I winna be able to bide it. Eh, mother, efter Steenie, it'll be awfu' to spen' the day wi 'ier! It's no 'at ever she'll be fou: I s' see to that! -- it's 'at she'll aye be toom! -- aye ringin wi toomness!"
texts.91.7: Here Kirsty turned to her father, and said, --
texts.91.8: "Wull ye gie me a tocher, father?"
texts.91.9: "Ay wull I, lassie, -- what ye like, sae far as I hae't to gie."
texts.91.10: "I want Donal -- that's a'. Ye see I maun ride a heap wi the puir thing, and I wud fain hae something aneth me 'at ye gae me! The cratur 'll aye hing to the Knowe, and, whan I gie his wull he'll fess me hame o' himsel. -- I wud hae likit things to bide as they are, but she wud hae worn puir Francie to the verra deid!"
texts.92.1: Mrs. Gordon manages the house and her reward is to sit at the head of the table, but she pays Kirsty infinitely more for the privilege than any but Kirsty can know, in the form of leisure for things she likes far better than housekeeping -- among the rest, for the discovery of such songs as this, the last of hers I have seen:--
texts.93.1: Love is the part, and Love is the whole;
texts.93.2: Love is the robe, and Love is the pall;
texts.93.3: Ruler of heart and brain and soul,
texts.93.4: Love is the Lord and the slave of all!
texts.93.5: I thank Thee, Love, that Thou lov'st me;
texts.93.6: I thank Thee more that I love Thee.
texts.93.7: Love is the rain, and Love is the air;
texts.93.8: Love is the earth that holdeth fast;
texts.93.9: Love is the root that is buried there.
texts.93.10: Love is the open flower at last!
texts.93.11: I thank Thee, Love all round about,
texts.93.12: That the eyes of my Love are looking out.
texts.93.13: Love is the sun and Love is the sea;
texts.93.14: Love is the tide that comes and goes;
texts.93.15: Flowing and flowing it comes to me;
texts.93.16: Ebbing and ebbing to thee it flows!
texts.93.17: Oh my sun, and my wind, and tide!
texts.93.18: My sea, and my shore, and all beside!
texts.93.19: Light, oh light that art by showing;
texts.93.20: Wind, oh wind that liv'st by motion;
texts.93.21: Thought, oh thought that art by knowing;
texts.93.22: Will, that art bom in self-devotion!
texts.93.23: Love is you, though not all of you know it;
texts.93.24: Ye are not love, yet ye always show it!
texts.93.27: Home to Thee all thy glories gather --
texts.93.28: All are Thy love, and there is no other!
texts.93.29: O Love-at-rest; we loves that roam --
texts.93.30: Home unto Thee, we are coming home!
